slides.title: Introduction to Parametric Tests
slides.text:
Introduction to Parametric Tests
What Are Parametric Tests?
Parametric tests are statistical tests that make specific assumptions about the parameters (e.g., mean, variance) and distribution (typically normal distribution) of the population from which the sample is drawn.
These tests are powerful and efficient when their assumptions are met, providing precise estimates.
Key Assumptions
Data is quantitative (interval or ratio scale)
Population follows a specific distribution (usually normal)
Homogeneity of variance: Variability is similar across groups
Independence of observations: Each data point is unrelated to the others

slides.title: Common Parametric Tests
slides.text:
Common Parametric Tests
t-Tests:
One-sample t-test: compares sample mean to a known population mean
Independent two-sample t-test: compares means of two independent groups
Paired t-test: compares means from the same group at different times or matched samples
Z-Test: Often for large samples, known population standard deviation
ANOVA (Analysis of Variance): Compares means across three or more groups (one-way, two-way ANOVA)
Pearson's Correlation (r): Measures the strength and direction of the linear relationship between two continuous variables

slides.title: When to Use Parametric Tests?
slides.text:
When to Use Parametric Tests?
Use parametric tests when:
Your data is continuous and approximately normally distributed
The sample size is moderate or large
Population parameters (like mean, variance) can be meaningfully estimated
Example
Comparing the mean test scores of two classes (independent t-test)
Testing whether the body temperatures of a group deviate from the standard 98.6°F (one-sample t-test)
Checking if multiple factories produce products with the same average weight (ANOVA)
Limitation: Violating assumptions (like normality or equal variances) can lead to misleading results. In such cases, non-parametric tests are recommended.

slides.title: Types of t-Tests
slides.text:
Types of t-Tests
One-Sample t-Test
Compares the mean of a single group to a known or hypothesised population mean.
Used when we want to know if our sample is significantly different from a specific value.
Independent Two-Sample t-Test (Unpaired)
Compares the means of two independent groups.
Used when samples come from different populations (e.g., Treatment vs Control).
Groups must be unrelated.
Paired (Dependent) t-Test
Compares the means from the same group at different times (pre/post) or matched pairs.
Used when measurements are repeated or pairs are naturally linked.

slides.title: Example (One-Sample t-Test)
slides.text:
Example (One-Sample t-Test)
A dietician says the average sugar content in an energy bar should be 15g.
You sample 10 bars: mean = 14g, standard deviation = 2g.
Is there evidence that the mean sugar is different from 15g at α=0.05?

bullets.text: A dietician says the average sugar content in an energy bar should be 15g.
You sample 10 bars: mean = 14g, standard deviation = 2g.
Is there evidence that the mean sugar is different from 15g at α=0.05?

slides.visual_text: Below the problem is a calculation box. Calculation: t = (14 - 15) / (2/√10) = -1/0.632 ≈ -1.58. Find degrees of freedom: df = 9. Compare to critical t (two-tailed, α = 0.05): ±2.685 (the 685 is typed over in a different font). Decision: |t| < 2.262 → Fail to reject the null hypothesis.

Example (Independent Two-Sample t-Test)
A researcher wants to compare test scores between two classes.
Class A: n=15, mean=78, SD=10
Class B: n=14, mean=85, SD=8

slides.visual_text: Below the data is a worked solution. Step 1: Calculate pooled SD: sp = √[((14)(10²) + (13)(8²)) / 27] = √[(1400 + 832) / 27] = √82.96 ≈ 9.1. Step 2: Compute t: t = (78 - 85) / (9.1 √(1/15 + 1/14)) = -7 / (9.1 × 0.38) = -7/3.46 ≈ -2.02. Degrees of freedom = 15+14-2 = 27. Critical t (two-tailed, α = 0.05) ≈ ±2.373 (the 373 is typed over in a different font). Decision: |t| < 2.052 → Fail to reject the null hypothesis.

slides.title: Example (Paired t-Test)
slides.text:
Example (Paired t-Test)
A fitness trainer wants to see if a training program reduces pulse rate.
6 clients: pulse before (72, 75, 70, 80, 78, 77), after (70, 76, 69, 78, 76, 75)
2.571

bullets.text: A fitness trainer wants to see if a training program reduces pulse rate.

slides.visual_text: Below the data is a worked solution. Sample size, n = 6 clients. Differences (Before - After): 2, -1, 1, 2, 2, 2. Mean difference, d̄ = 1.33. Standard deviation of differences, sd = 1.211. Step 1: State Hypotheses. Null hypothesis H0: the training program has no effect or does not reduce pulse rate, H0: μd = 0. Alternative hypothesis H1: the training program reduces pulse rate, H1: μd > 0. Step 2: Calculate the t-Statistic: t = (d̄ - μ0) / (sd/√n) = (1.33 - 0) / (1.211/√6) = 1.33/0.494 ≈ 2.69. Step 3: Degrees of Freedom: df = n - 1 = 6 - 1 = 5. Step 4: Determine Critical Value and P-value. For a one-tailed test with α = 0.05 and df = 5, the critical t-value t0.05,5 ≈ 2.571 (typed in a separate box). Calculated t = 2.69 > 2.015, so we reject the null hypothesis. P-value (one-tailed) corresponding to t = 2.69 and df = 5 is approximately 0.021 (less than 0.05). Step 5: Conclusion: There is statistically significant evidence at the 5% level that the training program reduces pulse rate.

slides.title: ANOVA or F-Test
slides.text:
ANOVA or F-Test
Developed by Sir Ronald Fisher
ANOVA stands for Analysis of Variance
It is a test of means for two or more samples. The null hypothesis, as usual, says that the means are equal.
The Dependent Variable has to be on a Metric Scale (Continuous Scale: Interval and Ratio Scale), and the Independent Variables have to be on a Non-Metric Scale (Categorical Scale: Nominal or Ordinal Scale)
The categorial independent variables are called Factors. One factor is one-way ANOVA, two factors are two-way ANOVA, etc.

bullets.text: Developed by Sir Ronald Fisher
ANOVA stands for Analysis of Variance
It is a test of means for two or more samples. The null hypothesis, as usual, says that the means are equal.

The Dependent Variable has to be on a Metric Scale (Continuous Scale: Interval and Ratio Scale), and the Independent Variables have to be on a Non-Metric Scale (Categorical Scale: Nominal or Ordinal Scale)
The categorial independent variables are called Factors. One factor is one-way ANOVA, two factors are two-way ANOVA, etc.

slides.title: Why Use ANOVA Instead of Multiple t-Tests?
slides.text:
Why Use ANOVA Instead of Multiple t-Tests?
Performing multiple t-tests increases Type I error risk
ANOVA keeps the overall error rate at the set significance level (e.g., 0.05)
Efficiently compares multiple means with a single test

slides.title: Key Concepts
slides.text:
Key Concepts
Between-group variance: Variation due to differences in group means
Within-group variance: Variation within each group due to random error
F-statistic: Ratio of between-group to within-group variance
Large F-value ⇒ high likelihood of significant difference among means

bullets.text: Between-group variance: Variation due to differences in group means
Within-group variance: Variation within each group due to random error
F-statistic: Ratio of between-group to within-group variance
Large F-value ⇒ high likelihood of significant difference among means

slides.title: Hypothesis Framework
slides.text:
Hypothesis Framework
For both One-Way and Two-Way ANOVA:
Null Hypothesis (H0): All group means are equal (μ1=μ2=...=μk)
Alternative Hypothesis (H1): At least one group mean differs
Decision Rule:
If Fcalculated>Fcritical or p<α: Reject H0

slides.title: Formulae
slides.text: Formulae
slides.visual_text: Heading: Formulae. A set of formula boxes. F = Variance between groups / Variance within groups. F = MSbetween / MSwithin, with labels: MSbetween is the Mean Sum of Squares between groups (variance between groups) and MSwithin is the Mean Sum of Squares within groups (variance within groups). MSbetween = SSbetween / dfbetween, with dfbetween = k - 1. MSwithin = SSwithin / dfwithin, with dfwithin = nT - k. Key: k = the number of groups (or levels); nT = the total number of participants across all groups (or levels); df = degrees of freedom, an estimation of sample size.

slides.title: Formulae
slides.text: Formulae
slides.visual_text: Heading: Formulae. Within Groups Variance = Σ(Xij - μj)² / (n - k). Between Groups Variance = Σ nj(μj - μt)² / (k - 1). ANOVA F statistic = Between Groups Variance / Within Groups Variance.

slides.title: Two-Way ANOVA
slides.text:
Two-Way ANOVA
Involves two independent variables (factors) and one dependent variable.
Allows for:
Main effects of each factor
Interaction effect between factors
Example: Does product quality (standard vs premium) and price level (low, medium, high) jointly affect purchase intention?
Hypotheses:
H01: No main effect of price
H02: No main effect of quality
H03: No interaction between price and quality

slides.title: Regression Analysis
slides.text:
Regression Analysis
A statistical method to examine the relationship between a dependent (Y) and an independent variable (X)
It helps predict the value of Y based on X
Example Applications:
Predicting sales from ad spending
Forecasting demand from price data
Estimating employee performance from training hours

bullets.text: A statistical method to examine the relationship between a dependent (Y) and an independent variable (X)
It helps predict the value of Y based on X
Example Applications:
Predicting sales from ad spending
Forecasting demand from price data
Estimating employee performance from training hours

slides.visual_text: Below the bullets is the equation Y = a + bX. Where: Y: Dependent variable (outcome); X: Independent variable (predictor); a: Intercept (value of Y when X = 0); b: Slope (change in Y for a unit change in X).

slides.title: The Regression Line
slides.text:
The Regression Line
Line of Best Fit: Represents the expected relationship between X and Y
Slope (b) shows direction and strength of the relationship
Positive b → Y increases with X
Negative b → Y decreases with X

bullets.text: Line of Best Fit: Represents the expected relationship between X and Y
Slope (b) shows direction and strength of the relationship
Positive b → Y increases with X
Negative b → Y decreases with X

slides.visual_text: Formula pictures between the bullets. Y = a + bX. b = [NΣXY - (ΣX)(ΣY)] / [NΣX² - (ΣX)²]. a = (ΣY - bΣX) / N. Where N = number of observations, or years; X = a year index (decade); Y = population size for given census years. A second formula for the slope: b = Σ(X - X̄)(Y - Ȳ) / Σ(X - X̄)².

slides.title: Alternate Formulae
slides.text:
Alternate Formulae
R-square is the Coefficient of Determination. It is the square of the correlation coefficient (r)
The higher the value of R-square, the higher the explanatory power of the independent variable for the dependent variable.

bullets.text: R-square is the Coefficient of Determination. It is the square of the correlation coefficient (r)
The higher the value of R-square, the higher the explanatory power of the independent variable for the dependent variable.

slides.visual_text: Formula pictures on the left: SSxy = Σxy - (Σx)(Σy)/n; SSxx = Σx² - (Σx)²/n; SSyy = Σy² - (Σy)²/n. On the right: b = SSxy / SSxx and r = SSxy / √(SSxx SSyy). The two bullets about R-square sit below them.

slides.title: Parametric vs. Non-Parametric Tests
slides.text:
Parametric vs. Non-Parametric Tests
Basis | Parametric Tests | Non-Parametric Tests
Data type | Interval or ratio (Continuous) | Ordinal or nominal
Distribution | Assumes normality | No assumption of distribution
Measure | Mean and SD | Medians and ranks
Example Tests | t-test, ANOVA, regression | Chi-square, Mann-Whitney, Wilcoxon, Kruskal-Wallis
Sample Size | Usually large | Works with small samples
Use When | Data is symmetric, continuous | Data is skewed or categorical

slides.title: Why Use Non-Parametric Tests?
slides.text:
Why Use Non-Parametric Tests?
Data does not meet parametric assumptions (normality, homogeneity)
Data is ordinal or categorical (ranked preferences, satisfaction ratings)
Small samples or outliers distort means
Useful in Six Sigma, quality control, customer satisfaction, or survey data environments.

bullets.text: Data does not meet parametric assumptions (normality, homogeneity)
Data is ordinal or categorical (ranked preferences, satisfaction ratings)
Small samples or outliers distort means
Useful in Six Sigma, quality control, customer satisfaction, or survey data environments.

slides.title: Key Non-Parametric Tests Overview
slides.text:
Key Non-Parametric Tests Overview
Test | Type | Used When | Business Application
Chi-square | Categorical | Compare observed vs expected frequencies | Market share, preference counts
Wilcoxon Signed-Rank | Dependent (paired) | Compare medians of matched data | Pre/post customer feedback
Mann-Whitney U | Independent | Test differences between two independent groups | Compare supplier ratings
Kruskal-Wallis | Multiple groups | Compare 3+ independent groups | Customer satisfaction across regions

Example
The Chi-square test is a test of independence
e.g., is there a relationship between variables or not?
By independence, we mean no relationship.
Null hypothesis: the two variables are statistically independent
H0: Watch Preference and Age are independent.
There is no relationship between them
Alternate Hypothesis: the variables are related, not independent of each other
H1: Watch preference and Age are dependent
